lines.text: Old kingdoms, a French colony, a cocoa boom and two civil wars. This is the story of Ivory Coast, on the Gulf of Guinea.
In the early seventeen hundreds the Kong Empire rose in the north, a Muslim state of traders and scholars.
In 1893 France made the coast a colony, and would rule it for almost seventy years.
Abidjan grew from a small settlement on a lagoon into the country's largest city.
Felix Houphouet-Boigny would lead the country to independence and rule it as president for thirty-three years.
Henri Konan Bedie would succeed him, and govern through the nineties.
Alassane Ouattara, an economist, would become president after the bitter election of 2010.
Laurent Gbagbo, his great rival, would hold the presidency from 2000 to 2011.
Alpha Blondy would make Ivory Coast a home of African reggae.
In 1960 Ivory Coast became independent, and it went on to become the world's largest grower of cocoa.
For two decades cocoa and coffee brought fast growth, and people spoke of the Ivorian miracle.
In 1972 Tai National Park was created to protect one of the last great rainforests of West Africa.
Didier Drogba, a striker of world renown, would use his fame to call for an end to the fighting.
Yaya Toure would be named African footballer of the year four times.
In 1983 the capital moved to Yamoussoukro, the president's home village.
There, in 1989, the Basilica of Our Lady of Peace was finished, one of the largest churches in the world.
In 2002 Abidjan gave birth to coupe-decale, dance music that spread across Africa.
That same year civil war broke out, splitting the country in two until 2007.
In 2006 toxic waste from a ship was dumped around Abidjan, and thousands of people fell ill.
After the disputed election of 2010, war returned, until Gbagbo was removed in 2011.
And in early 2024 Ivory Coast hosted the Africa Cup of Nations, and won it on home soil.
From the Kong Empire to a home victory, Ivory Coast keeps building peace on its cocoa wealth.
